title: disk-io-scheduler-ssd-queue-depth-investigation-notes
content:
Summary:

Observed a recurring cluster-wide spike in pod start latency and kubelet heartbeat jitter on a subset of GPU-backed worker nodes in us-west-2 between 2025-11-05 and 2025-11-06. Symptoms aligned with high iowait and long block device queues on /dev/nvme1n1. The pattern correlated with periodic background compaction/flush activity from local RocksDB instances belonging to several stateful workloads and with short bursts of many small random writes from logging/sidecar agents.

Key impact:
- ~20% increase in pod start 95p latency for batch inference pods (30s -> 36s) during windows.
- Kubelet syncs delayed; node became NotReady briefly in 6/24 affected nodes due to probe failures.
- Pod restarts on system-critical daemonsets (cni-plugin, node-exporter) observed on 3 nodes.

Initial indicators and metrics observed:
- Node-level iowait spiking to 60-80% for 30-120s windows (node exporter, 1s scrape).
- blkio queue depth (/sys/block/nvme1n1/queue/nr_requests) observed at sustained ~1024 during bursts (default NVMe qdepth 1024 on our kernel).
- iostat -x sample (one 60s burst):
  Device: rrqm/s wrqm/s r/s w/s rkB/s wkB/s rrqms rawait wawait aqu-sv
  nvme1n1 0.00 0.00 10.50 420.40 80.2 13040 0.00 12.4 45.3 60.2
- blktrace samples showed many synchronous small writes (~4KB-16KB) from containers with hostPath-mounted log folders.
- Kubelet logs: repeated kubelet sync loops with 100ms -> 5s delays, causing liveness probe failures for some system pods.

Hypothesis / Root cause (current):
A combination of workload-level micro-IO patterns (many small fsync/pwrite operations) plus RocksDB compaction spikes created transient but large concurrency of block requests. This saturated the device queue depth and caused the kernel block layer and NVMe driver to spend long time scheduling and waiting, raising iowait and delaying critical system processes (kubelet, CNI). On top of that, we lack cgroup-level IO limits for those containers (cgroup v2 io.max not configured), so noisy tenants can blow out a node's device queue.

Why this matters for Kubernetes:
- Kubelet and system agents are CPU + IO sensitive; when IO stalls, heartbeats and probe handlers are delayed -> kube-controller marks node NotReady or pods get restarted.
- Scheduler backpressure: slow kubelet reconciles cause increased pod start latency and scheduling piling up.

What we ran and immediate triage steps taken (timeline):
- 2025-11-05 02:10 UTC: Pager fired (alert: node_iowait_percent > 40% for 2m).
- 02:14: Collected: top, iostat -x 1 60, sar -u, blktrace (20s), dmesg tail. Snapshotted /proc/interrupts, /sys/block/*/queue/* values.
- 02:25: Identified noisy containers via iotop + lsof: logging-sidecar (container id abc123) and stateful-app (idx-6) writing small fsyncs.
- 02:30: Temporarily cordoned two worst nodes and migrated non-critical pods to others (kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data).
- 02:40: Reduced logging sidecar verbosity and rotated logs to limit fsync frequency.
- 03:05: Temporarily applied per-node io.max via systemd slice housekeeping (see mitigation below) to keep kubelet/system pods responsive.

Short-term mitigations applied (post-incident):
- Added emergency cgroup v2 io.max throttles for the noisy units via a systemd drop-in for the workload's unit on affected nodes (io.max set to 20mb 400iops as stopgap). This reduced observed iowait and restored kubelet heartbeat stability.
- Tuned kubelet eviction thresholds to be slightly more conservative for ephemeral-storage/available and nodefs to avoid premature pod evictions while we measured root cause.
- Adjusted logging agent config across the cluster (deploy-rollback for a lighter config) to buffer writes and flush less frequently.

Longer-term remediation recommendations:
1) Platform-level I/O QoS:
   - Adopt cgroup v2 io.max limits for noisy system/tenant workloads by default (policy: system pods unlimited; best-effort tenants restricted). Add this to node bootstrap image and DaemonSet that opt-in workloads can use.
   - For EBS-backed instance groups: ensure block device provisioning (gp3) has IOPS/throughput aligned with expected workload; consider per-node mapping and alerts when queue depth > X for > Y seconds.

2) Kernel and queue tuning:
   - Evaluate lowering default queue depth on our worker images for nvme devices (e.g. /sys/block/nvme*/queue/nr_requests = 512) and test latency impact.
   - Investigate blk-mq scheduler tweaks (e.g. rq_affinity) and IO scheduler selection (none/none for NVMe). Document a safe tuning matrix per instance family.

3) Workload changes / guidance:
   - Update internal SLO docs to recommend burst-aware write amplification patterns (batching + append-only logging).
   - For stateful stores (RocksDB), coordinate compaction windows (stagger across replicas) and enable compaction throttling where possible.
   - Encourage use of ephemeral devices with filesystem mount options tuned for many small writes (discard, noatime, journal options), and recommend tmpfs for transient high-churn logs when appropriate.

4) Observability and alerts:
   - Add alert: block_queue_depth_high (per-device) when nr_requests > 800 for > 60s.
   - Add node-level SRE dashboard: iowait, device queue depth, io.util, avg_queue_size, slow-io-pod-list.
   - Create a tiny exporter that surfaces top IO-generating containers per node (iostat + /proc/<pid>/io correlation).

Playbook (runbook) draft for on-call when similar fires:
1) Pager: node_iowait_percent > 40% for 2m or device queue depth alert.
2) Immediately collect: top, iostat -x 1 30, iotop -oPa, ss, dmesg, kubectl get nodes, kubectl describe node <node>.
3) Identify top writers by container PID: use pidstat -d -p ALL and /proc/*/io cross-check.
4) If noisy non-system containers found: try to temporarily scale down or kill the workload; if it's a system workload, apply temporary io.max via systemd on that unit.
5) If kubelet is unhealthy: cordon node, drain non-critical pods, and verify kubelet service restart (systemctl restart kubelet) only after ensuring storage mounts are stable.
6) Post-stabilization: capture blktrace for 60s, save /var/log/messages, and create an incident ticket with all artifacts.

Open questions / research tasks:
- How many other instance types show similar behaviour by default? (need matrix of NVMe devices and default qdepths across instance families)
- Is there an upstream kernel version where NVMe queue handling was fixed/improved for small-sync writes? Should we bump node kernel?
- How will io.max interact with existing sandbox/container runtime (runc/crun) on our images? Edge cases for devices used in multiple containers (hostPath).

Concrete follow-ups and owners (next 30d):
- SRE: implement device queue depth alerting + dashboard (Owner: Raj Patel, ETA: 2025-11-20).
- Infra: test lowering /sys/block/*/queue/nr_requests on a canary pool and measure pod start latency under synthetic small-write load (Owner: Tom Bowers, ETA: 2025-11-27).
- Platform/DevEx: publish guidance for RocksDB compaction staggering and logging-sidecar config recommendations (Owner: Lina Gomez, ETA: 2025-11-18).
- Security/Ops: harden systemd slice presets for critical pods so they remain unaffected by io.max in emergency (Owner: Maya Chen, ETA: 2025-12-02).

Notes / artifacts attached:
- Blktrace sample logs saved to gs://redwood-sre-artifacts/2025-11-05/disk-io-bursts-node-17.tar.gz
- Collected metrics charts: dashboard link (internal) -> https://grafana.redwood.local/d/cluster/disk-io-bursts
- JIRA ticket: SRE-1342 (tracking remediation).

Appendix: useful commands executed during triage (examples)
- iostat -x 1 60
- sudo blktrace -d /dev/nvme1n1 -o - | blkparse -i - -d 30 > /tmp/blktrace-node17.txt
- sudo cat /sys/block/nvme1n1/queue/nr_requests
- sudo bash -c 'echo "8:0 20971520" > /sys/fs/cgroup/io.max'  # example io.max via unified cgroup (illustrative)
- sudo iotop -oPa -b -n 10 > /tmp/iotop-node17.txt

Closing note:
This incident is a useful reminder that high-throughput spike patterns are not only a network/CPU problem — block layer and device queue tuning are critical for latency-sensitive control-plane processes. We should treat IO QoS as a first-class dimension of node capacity planning.

Draft status: working notes to be matured into a full post-incident review. Please add any additional logs/artifacts to the JIRA ticket and comment on the proposed runbook changes.
